IN H! within the next quarter century. Surface coatings will be the principal consumer of these aromatic chemicals. 

The lower aromatics may be synthesized in several different ways and from various petroleum components. It is outside the scope of this study to forecast the utilization of aromatics raw materials from the standpoint of economics. However, the most important method today is dehydrogenation of naphthenes by catalytic reforming of selected virgin naphtha fractions. Isomerization to convert methylcyclopentane to cyclohexane may be integrated with low-pressure catalytic reforming to maximize benzene. Similarly, in producing toluene, the dimethylcyclopentane must be isomerized first to methylcyclohexane.

Isomerization and dehydrogenation can be made to proceed simultaneously. This is done by the "hydroforming process" under relatively high pressures and in the presence of recycled hydrogen. Supported molybdenum, tungsten, chromium, or platinum catalysts are employed. Two process improvements in hydroforming are (a) "platforming," which uses a platinum catalyst at high pressure, and (b) "fluid" hydroforming, which uses powdered catalysts containing molybdenum or other metals at lower pressure. Both "platforming" and two-step isomerization-hydroforming are used commercially today. 

Based on potential raw material, catalytic cyclization of normal hexane to benzene and normal heptane to toluene may be important processes in the future. Another possible synthesis is dealkylation of alkylated aromatics. Some aromatics are available as byproducts from severe high-temperature cracking of oils for the production of unsaturates. Catalytic naphtha contains only small amounts of benzene and toluene and has not been of much interest. Also crude oils contain benzene and toluene in small amounts. Benzene contents range from 0.001 to 0.4 percent. Special recovery of these lower aromatics from crudes are likely to be of economic interest only when combined with aromatics synthesis operations.

All of the above syntheses require a further processing step to purify the aromatics for use as chemicals. The contaminants may be saturated hydrocarbons or they may be olefins and diolefins. Extractive distillation, solvent extraction, and silica gel adsorption are the present commercially available techniques. 

Returning to the question of aromatics supply, it would appear that the potential benzene supply, through the various routes described, could be four- or five-fold the predicted 1975 demand. In the case of toluene and xylenes, aviation gasoline will require a share. However, after satisfying probable aviation requirements it is estimated that chemicals will require less than 10 percent of the remainder. This is an important consideration from the standpoint of meeting future motor gasoline quality.

FORECASTS 

The estimated hydrocarbon raw-material requirements for petrochemicals have been based on forecasts of petrochemicals, together with end-use patterns, which were prepared by the 

Chemical Products Department of the Esso Standard Oil Co. 

These are summarized in table V. Estimated future requirements of synthetic fibers and plastics were supplied by N. M. 

Elias of the President's Materials Policy Commission and are understood to represent a concensus of industry. These two end-use groups have determined the forecasts of many of the major petrochemicals. Notably, ethylene and benzene requirements are markedly sensitive to changes in the plastics picture. 

Approximately one-half of the hydrocarbon raw materials requirements in 1975 are for resins and plastics.

Referring to table V, it should be appreciated that the quantity of primary products shown for a particular end-use group is not the quantity of end-use products. Also it should be understood that these primary products represent only those derived from petroleum and natural gas.

It will be noted that for most end-use groups the weight of the primary products is greater than the weight of the hydrocarbon raw material. The general explanation of this, which applies to all groups excepting synthetic rubber, lies in the fact that many of the primary products are formed by the addition of nonhydrocarbon material to the hydrocarbon. As examples, the various alcohols, ethylene oxide, ethylene glycol and glycerine, all include oxygen; other products include chlorine or bromine. Ammonia is largely nitrogen, with the hydrogen only being derived from hydrocarbons. Here the primary products include an unavoidable duplication arising through consideration of both benzene derived from petroleum and all of the styrene as primary products. Styrene is considered as a primary product of ethylene. However, the benzene going into styrene includes a proportionate share of coal tar benzene.

The only other duplication in primary products occurs in the case of cumene, which is made by alkylating benzene with propylene. Both cumene and benzene are primary products. 

However, there are no duplications in hydrocarbon raw materials. 

In addition to the general assumptions which were made to establish the over-all pattern of this survey, certain other conditions have been defined to limit the scope of the forecasts and to set the course of future trends. a) The forecasts have been restricted to nonfuel uses of petroleum raw materials. Thus, aromatics for use in aviation gasoline have been excluded. b) Abnormal requirements of chemicals (e. g., toluene and ammonia) for explosives have been excluded. c) Petroleum byproducts such as sulfur and helium have not been included. d) Excluded also are requirements of heavy oils and natural gas for the manufacture of carbon black. e) Gradual eclipse of fermentation ethanol by synthetics has been assumed. f) Virtually all increases in aromatics are assumed to come from petroleum. g) It has been assumed that natural gas will gradually supplant coke as a source of synthesis gas for methanol and ammonia. h) Additional rubber requirements will be mainly synthetic and probably the new capacity will be largely for improved types over Buna-S. i) Due consideration has been given to the critical shortages of sulfur and chlorine. Thus, it has been assumed that manufacture of phenol by the cumene hydroperoxide synthesis will become increasingly important as compared to the benzene chlorination and sulfonation methods. j) It is visualized that the detergents industry will continue to enjoy a vigorous growth. This will limit the availability of byproduct glycerine from soap manufacture and require increasing production of synthetic glycerine from petroleum. k) Acetylene is expected to become an important petrochemical raw material. Petroleum acetylene by partial oxidation of methane or regenerative cracking of propane now offers a potentially cheaper source of supply than calcium carbide. 

It is assumed that future increases in acetylene requirements for chemical synthesis will be largely from petroleum sources. 

Very approximate investment figures for new petrochemical plants have been prepared. These are summarized in table VI. 

They are presented for 5-year periods ending in 1955, 1960, etc. The 1955 investments include many new plants now under construction or for which construction has been approved. 

Tables VII and VIII summarize the utilities and fuel requirements, respectively, for the end-use groups. The figures shown represent the total requirements for both existing and new plants at the end of 1955, 1960, etc. For each of these years, the distribution was made in accordance with the end-use pattern which was established for the apportionment of hydrocarbon raw materials and investments. Approximately 89 percent of the petrochemical production is represented. 

The utilities requirements allow for about 37 percent capacity above the predicted normal stream day demands. This provides an allowance for uncertainties in the demand plus such spare capacity as may be required to insure an uninterrupted supply of utilities to the operating units. This is consistent with good manufacturing practice. The electricity requirements include power for pumping cooling water.

In the case of fuel, a breakdown is given between direct and indirect fuel. Direct fuel is that consumed in furnaces or for the operation of gas engine driven compressors. Indirect fuel is that required for the generation of steam and power. Fuel has been expressed as millions of British thermal units per calen. dar day. Fuel has not been included for the spare steam and power generating capacity. Fuel requirements may be converted to equivalent fuel oil on the basis of 6.3 million B. t. u.'s per barrel (42 gallons) of fuel oil or to equivalent natural gas by allowing 1,080 B. t. u.'s per standard cubic foot of natural gas. 

Table IX presents a very rough estimate of the metals required for the construction of petrochemical plants covering about 89 percent of the petrochemical operations. This is based on experience within this company and includes representative types of plants. The metals are grouped into four broad classes as follows: (a) steel, (b) cast iron, (c) ferrous alloys (including stainless steels and the like), and (d) nonferrous metals (e. g., copper, lead, bronzes, etc.). 

The requirements shown provide for onsite, offsite, and utilities sections of the plants. Also they include machinery (pumps, compressors, motors, etc.) as well as towers, reactors, piping, structural steel, and such.

Although the nonferrous metals represent a very broad group, it has not been feasible to make a more detailed breakdown.

The Promise of Technology The Possibilities of Solar Energy* Chapter 15 

IN THE FIRST 182 centuries of this era, the total input to the energy system of the world was about 6Q,† equivalent to some 225 billion short tons of bituminous coal. In the next century, ending in 1950, we burned up 4Q—more than half as much. 

In 1850 the annual input was at the rate of about 1.0Q a century. In 1950 the rate had multiplied 10 times—to some 380 billion tons of coal equivalent a century. 

The requirements per capita for the output of energy at the various points of end-use-as, for example, the draw-bar of a locomotive-have been growing strongly. 

The world growth-rate has averaged about 2.2 percent a year compounded since 1860. It has tended to increase quite steadily. During the past 15 years its growth has been at the rate of about 3 percent. The rate is probably continuing to increase.

In the United States the per capita requirements for the output of energy has grown a little more swiftly than has the average world rate. The growth-rate has averaged about 3.4 percent since 1897. During the past 15 years it has averaged nearly 4 percent. The rate is probably continuing to increase. 

Estimates of the trends in three quantities are necessary to an estimate of future over-all requirements for input of energy. 

The three quantities are: The per capita demand for the output of energy; the efficiency with which energy is used; the population. A discussion of over-all energy demands will be found in "Projection of 1975 Materials Demand," in volume II. 

If we are to avoid the risk of seriously increased real unit costs of energy in the United States, then new low-cost sources should be made ready to pick up some of the load by 1975. 

ENERGY FROM THE SUN 

The intensity of solar radiation, measured outside the earth's atmosphere, at mean solar distance, is 7.15 British thermal units per square foot per minute, or the equivalent of seventenths of a ton of bituminous coal per acre per hour. The sunlight intercepted by the earth at the outer boundaries of the atmosphere in 1 year has an energy content of about 5,300Qmore than 200,000 billion short tons of bituminous coal. *This paper, condensed by the Commission's staff, is based on a draft memorandum prepared for the Commission by Palmer Putnam, former consultant to the Atomic Energy Commission. It is included in this volume to indicate the limits of present knowledge of solar energy as well as the frontiers for future technology. +1.0Q=1.0x10¹8 B. t. u., equivalent to some 38 billion short tons of bituminous coal.

A thick cloud reflects about three-fourths of the sunlight that strikes it. The water vapor and the other ingredients of the atmosphere absorb and reflect up to one-fourth of the incoming sunlight. In general, the solar energy that reaches horizontal surfaces in the lower middle latitudes is equivalent to about 1,000 tons of coal per acre per year—about 2.75 tons per day.

In summer, in the arid sub-tropics, the average daily rate is equivalent to about 3.7 tons of coal per acre per day. The maximum rate may reach 5 tons on a clear, dry day in June. 

The average for the United States is about 800 tons of coal per acre per year.

These are convenient yardsticks for evaluating proposals for harnessing sunlight.

The area of the United States is about 2 billion acres, on which there falls, in an average year, sunlight with an energy content equal to that of about 1,900 billion tons of bituminous. coal. The input to the energy system of the United States in 1947 was equivalent to about 1,300 million tons of bituminous coal. 

So, the United States supply of solar energy is about 1,500 times the present requirement.

In middle latitudes, the natural conversion of sunlight by biological photosynthesis operates with an average annual efficiency of the order of 0.1 percent. The total carbon fixed in the 

United States in 1947 by photosynthesis would, if burned, have yielded less than the equivalent of 1,900 million tons of bituminous coal, or about 1.4 times our total energy requirements in 1947. Page 213

If our expanding energy system is ever to be largely dependent upon photosynthesis, we must devise great improvements over nature's method of harnessing sunlight. 

METHODS NOW IN USE 

There are various designs for solar hot-water heaters. One design, which illustrates the principle, consists of a system of pipes, backed by a black surface, the whole enclosed under glass, and mounted on a slanting roof that faces south. There are 4 to 5 lineal feet of three-fourths-inch pipe per square foot of glass area. 

Rule of thumb indicates that about 1 square foot of the pipeabsorber-glass area will produce a gallon of 180 degree Fahrenheit water daily during 7 or 8 months of the year in Miami, Fla. 

Each gallon-day of capacity represents a heat absorption of about 1,000 B. t. u. per day. The claim that 1,000 B. t. u. are absorbed per square foot daily implies an efficiency in Miami, Fla., or La Jolla, Calif., of over 45 percent, to be compared with efficiencies of 30 to 50 percent reported by Hottel and Telkes in the case of the solar houses designed at the Massa chusetts Institute of Technology. 

In rural areas where there are no washing machines, average demands for hot water are about 100 gallons a day for a family of five. Automatic clothes-washing and dish-washing demand greater quantities of hot water.

In 1939, nonfreeze commercial solar water heaters could be installed for about $8 per gallon-day of capacity. The nonfreeze type can be assumed to be fully operative about 270 days a year. The indicated cost is about $1.70 per million B. t. u. [2]. 

INDIRECT COLLECTION BY MEANS OF HEAT PUMP 

A heat pump is a device for collecting heat at a low temperature from well-water, the earth, or the air and delivering it at a higher temperature. One collection and concentration is usually done by an electrically operated pump.

The ratio of usefulness is the rates of energy spent in "pumping" to energy in the heat delivered.

Among the 500 heat pumps now in operation in the United 

States-25 industrial, 260 commercial and 215 residentialmany are operating at ratios of 4 to 1 and some at ratios of 

6 to 1.

The energy that is "mined" by the heat pump may be used for heating in winter, or for air-conditioning in summer. Both are accomplished without combustion, and so without odors, dirt, soot, or chimney.

The heat pump may also be used for making hot water, or for industrial processes such as drying, evaporation, and distillation.

The long mild winters and warm, humid summers of the 

South and Far West are most favorable for heat-pump installations. 

Solar energy may be used directly as the heat source for a heat pump. There is a technical reason why such a combination is attractive. It permits a low temperature in the solar collector, leading to a higher efficiency.

Chemical storage of heat may also be used in partnership with the heat-pump. Experimental installations reported by

Telkes indicate important savings in the combined first investment.

The first investment cost of a heat-pump is estimated to be about three times that of a conventional heating unit. Its economic justification rests on the availability of cheap electric power, in an area where fuel costs are high. Its thermodynamic cycle perhaps limits its application to uncongested areas. For example, the entire requirements of New York City for comfort heating and hot-water heating could hardly be taken from the water supply; or from the ground without lowering the frost line; or from the air without affecting the local climate.

METHODS NOT YET ECONOMICAL 

About a third of the energy system of the United States is devoted to comfort heating. Solar energy holds great promise in this field.

A solar heating installation is similar to the solar hot-water heater now used in parts of the South. 

A blackened flat plate faces south, at a selected angle of tilt toward the sun. The back side is insulated, to prevent "bottom" losses. On the front side are tubes or fins for the extraction of energy by a stream of heated air, water, or other fluid. The front side is covered by two or three air-spaced glass plates that pass the incoming short waves of solar energy, but prevents the re-radiation of the longer waves of heat.

Usually the collector is fixed. A solar tracking device is somewhat more efficient but much more costly.

Three types of collectors have been built. Their character istics are summarized in table III. 

Page 214

An experimental roof-type collector with hot water storage was built at M. I. T. in 1939. A blackened copper sheet with an area of 360 square feet was mounted on the roof, behind three air-spaced glass plates in insulated boxes. Copper tubes, soldered to the copper sheet, circulated water to a 17,000gallon insulated tank occupying the entire basement. The experimental two-room structure was heated entirely by solar energy during two heating seasons. A maximum storage temperature of 195 degrees Fahrenheit was reached during the summer, when the efficiency of the combined collector-storage system approached zero. The winter minimum temperature was about 125 degrees Fahrenheit.

Löf, at the University of Colorado, has been investigating a roof-type glass panel collector that circulates hot air. With an average daily exit air temperature of 110 degrees Fahrenheit, an efficiency of 35 to 40 percent could be obtained, but at higher temperatures the efficiency decreased considerably.

Solar houses using large south-facing windows have been tested at the Illinois Institute of Technology near Chicago, and at Purdue University. Most of the south wall of each house was occupied by air-spaced sealed double-glass windows, transmitting solar energy into the rooms. The houses had conventional radiant heating systems installed in the floors. On clear winter days these houses became overheated. Total fuel savings may have been as high as 30 percent. 

From these experiments the following conclusions have been drawn: a) It was possible to heat an experimental structure entirely with solar energy. b) Long-term heat-storage, as from summer to winter, is not economical. c) Fuel savings up to 30 percent can be realized when there is no special facility for heat storage. d) Heat storage at high temperature is inefficient and unnecessary. e) Large glass windows give glare on bright days and their fish-bowl effect causes a loss of privacy.

EFFICIENCIES 

By efficiency is meant the ratio between the solar energy striking the collector and the quantity that the collector passes into the house.

The efficiency of a solar-collector for house heating is high if the collector temperature is low. At Boston in December- 

January, when solar energy averages 1,000 B. t. u. per square foot a day, the efficiency of a wall or roof collector was 56 percent at a collector temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit; half this at 125 degrees Fahrenheit; and zero at 160 degrees Fahrenheit. 

The efficiency is high if the solar radiation is high. On clear winter days in Boston, when the solar energy averaged 1,500

B. t. u. per square foot per day, the efficiency at a collector temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit was 61 percent.

On cloudy days the efficiency of collection will be zero unless some threshold amount of solar energy is received. With a collector temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit, net collection begins at 168 B. t. u. per square foot per day. But with a collector temperature of 160 degrees Fahrenheit, there will be no net collection of heat until incoming solar energy amounts to 710 B. t. u. per square foot per day. These values are shown in table IV, for two glass plates, air-spaced. 

TABLE IV. Values of solar energy at which net collection of heat begins, in a 2-glass air-spaced collector at various collector temperatures [4] 

Collector temperature 

Daily solar energy • F. B. t. u./ square foot 70 90 130 160 22300 168 270 500 710 There are several possibilities for improving these efficiencies, suggested by Hottel.

First, these results have been obtained with common window glass, which contains some iron. The iron absorbs and reradiates outward about 4 percent of incoming solar energy. 

An iron-free glass probably could be obtained at no increase in cost if made up in large quantities. 

Second, window glass reflects about 4 percent of the incoming solar energy. A low-cost quarter wavelength coating is feasible. Such a coating would halve the reflection, reducing it to 2 percent.

These two modifications, taken together, would halve the outward heat losses caused by the glass. The average efficiency for a given collector temperature would be increased. The threshold at which collection could begin, however, would be decreased. 

A third possibility is a collector with factory-sealed edges, the spaces between filled, not with air, but with an inert gas having a thermal conductivity one-third that of air. 

These three modifications taken together would give an efficiency of some 65 percent or more during winter in Boston, with a collector temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit.

A fourth possibility is to use a plastic in lieu of glass, and to cast it in certain special and advantageous shapes for example, with ridges on the underside to focus sunlight along a line. The pipe of circulating fluid is located on the line. In this way useful temperatures for space heating can be obtained when the sun is so obscured by clouds that ordinary flat plate collectors would fail to operate.

Many other possibilities must be explored before the best design is found. 995554°-52-15 Page 215

HEAT STORAGE 

Heat may be stored in one of two ways. The first relies on the specific heat effect; the second on some chemical physical change of state.

If a cubic foot of water, with an initial temperature of 80 degrees Fahrenheit, should be brought up to a temperature of 

100 degrees Fahrenheit, the water would absorb some 1,300

B. t. u. Similarly, a cubic foot of concrete would absorb 1,000 

B. t. u. and scrap iron about 1,200 B. t. u.

Most solids require heat in order to be melted. The same amount of heat must be given up when the liquid solidifies. 

There are many salts with melting points which lie between room temperature and the temperatures at which solar energy may be conveniently collected. Because some of these salts are abundant low cost byproducts, Dr. Maria Telkes has proposed that they be used for the storage of heat [5]. One of these compounds is Glauber's salt—a hydrous sodium sulphate. This salt melts at about 90 degrees Fahrenheit, and in so doing requires 

9,500 B. t. u. per cubic foot.

The total amount of heat required to raise a cubic foot of 

Glauber's salt from 80 degrees Fahrenheit to 100 degrees is shown in table V. 

TABLE V.—Heat required to raise one cubic foot of Glauber's salt from 80° to 100° F. 

Below the melting point. 

At the melting point.. 

Above the melting point....

600 B. t. u. sp. ht. effect. 

9, 500 B. t. u. ht. of fusion effect. 

900 B. t. u. sp. ht. effect. 

11, 000 B. t. u.

So, assuming that Glauber's salt melts and recrystallizes without any time or temperature lag, it can effectively store about 7.8 times more heat than water, and the bulk of this heat is stored at a constant temperature of 90 degrees Fahrenheit.

The advantages of this type of chemical storage, as compared with specific heat storage, are as follows: a) A chemical compound, because of its latent heat of fusion, can store about seven times as much heat per unit volume as a substance responding solely to the specific heat effect. b) The chemical compound can collect solar heat at a constant moderate temperature. c) The threshold value for a collection temperature of 90 degrees Fahrenheit was seen to be 270 B. t. u. per square foot per day, compared with a threshold of some 500 B. t. u. per square foot per day with a collection temperature of 130 degrees Fahrenheit. This means that Glauber's salt can store solar energy on a dull day when a collector operating at a higher temperature would be imperative. 

The disadvantages of chemical heat storage are: a) The chemical compound must be put up in a very large number of quite small, permanently sealed containers. The cost of the containers is at least comparable with the cost of a water tank. b) There is a tendency for the chemical salt to stratify in the container, resulting in imperfect reversibility-something that can probably be minimized and overcome effectively by suitable design.

In a house that is to be heated entirely by solar energy, it will be necessary to provide storage not only for the cloudy days of an average winter, but also for the extra cloudiness of unusual winters.

Maria Telkes has concluded that in the Boston area storage for 9 consecutive days is adequate.

In Boston during December-January, the solar energy transmitted daily by 1 square foot of solar-collector can be stored in 63 pounds of Glauber's salt occupying a volume of 0.69 cubic foot, in a container 12 x 12 x 8.25 inches. 

Therefore, 600 cubic feet of Glauber's salt are required in the Boston area to carry the December-January heating load of a 15,000-cubic-foot house. A solar-heat-storage wall 9 inches thick could contain the 28 tons of Glauber's salt-16 tons of water and 12 tons of anhydrous sodium sulphate or "salt cake." The cost of the unpackaged cake in 1947 was approximately $240.

The seasonal heat load for such a properly constructed solar house in the Boston area is about 100 million B. t. u. The house could be entirely heated by solar energy falling on a two-glass plate collector with an area of 800 square feet. 

SOLAR ENERGY FOR COMFORT HEATING 

A well-insulated 15,000-cubic-foot house in Boston is estimated to require about 1,000 gallons of fuel oil a year, assuming a heating efficiency of 70 percent. At 13 cents a gallon, the annual fuel cost would be $130, which, capitalized at 10 percent, would amount to $1,300. The total investment in an oil burner system, including the burner, storage tanks and hotair ducts, is estimated at roughly $1,000. Thus, the total justified capital investment in a solar heating system would be not far from $2,300 in the Boston area—about 15 cents per cubic foot of house volume.

If the house is functionally designed for solar heating, and if the storage and collector elements are incorporated into the structure of the house as structural members, they should perhaps be credited with some small saving in building materialsperhaps as much as 1.6 cents a cubic foot. It seems to be the case that, throughout the South, solar heaters of domestic hot water have been successfully sold at prices somewhat in excess of the "justifiable investment," because the purchasers were willing to pay a premium for convenience, and, perhaps, for some psychological satisfactions. There is little reason to doubt that consumer responses would be similar in the case of a solar installation that would completely free the householder from all fuels except those desired for an open fire.

Without a more detailed feasibility and market analysis than has been possible in the preparation of this memorandum, it is impossible to say how good the Boston area is as a yardstick for measuring the national market for solar heating. In some other parts of the country the heating requirements would be less, which means that the fuel credits would be less, although the oil-burner credit would remain constant.

On balance, and subject to revision when a detailed feasibility and market analysis is prepared, it may be concluded that throughout most of the area of the 13 Southern States and some of the area in the middle tier of States, the owner of a new house would feel justified in investing between 20 and 30 cents per cubic foot of house volume in a solar heating system designed to carry the entire winter heating load.

Page 216

Cost studies reflecting the mass production of solar heating systems are not yet available. Hottel at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Löf at the University of Colorado both think that eventually systems could be marketed in mass production for about $3 per square foot of collector area. If a satisfactory plastic could be found to substitute for the glass, costs might be reduced.

MARKET FOR SOLAR COMFORT HEATING 

In the United States in 1950, comfort heating accounted for roughly one-third of the total energy requirements. 

Of new dwelling units to be built in the United States by 1975, some 30 percent probably will lie north of the critical line-in New England, the East North Central States, and the 

West North Central States. [6] 

Perhaps half of the remaining 70 percent will be isolated or small buildings, suitable for solar comfort heating. The assumption that solar collectors for space heating will be applicable only to individual isolated dwelling units, and not to apartment houses, or to rows of attached dwellings, may be incorrect. 

It is possible to conceive of apartment houses located in the middle and southern tiers of States, and functionally designed for solar heating. If so, the maximum plausible market may be more than 13 million installations, selling in the range of $2,000 to $3,000 each, and supporting about 10 percent of the national energy system.

Average costs of the natural water supply in 404 cities come to about $51 per acre foot. The cost of fresh water produced in a compression still is about $400 an acre foot, of which about 24 percent is charged off to the fuel account. A flat-plate solar still may not cost more than $1.00 per square foot (optimistically low) if it is to compete with a compression still, and not more than about 12 cents per square foot if it is to compete with natural water supplies.

DIRECT CONCENTRATION OF SUN ENERGY FOR POWER 

To obtain power from sunlight efficiently, it is necessary to concentrate its heat in some way in order to produce the optimum temperature of some 400 degrees Fahrenheit.

A plant designed by Shuman was erected near Cairo, Egypt, before 1914. It was used for a time to provide energy for irrigation from the Nile. 

C. G. Abbot of the Smithsonian Institution has proposed the use of cylindrical parabolic mirrors that follow the sun's path. In this method a dark oil is heated and then passed through a heat exchanger to make steam. The boiler efficiency is estimated to be about 60 percent, and the over-all efficiency of the reciprocating steam engine about 16 percent. 

Abbot doubts that units much greater than 5 horsepower would be found desirable, because of the requirement of 50 square feet of mirror per horsepower.

The Russians have reported that they are operating large units to harness solar energy in dry, fuel-short Uzbekistan, using large but simple fixed parabaloidal mirrors that give an efficiency of 10 percent.

The figures in table VII suggest that collectors of solar power, to be economical, are pretty well limited to cloudless regions of low latitude. These regions rarely support industrial complexes.

Thus the efficiency of an insulated still may be calculated at 68 percent. Of the losses listed in the table those of the transparent surface, the blacked surface, and resulting from re-radiation and air circulation, cannot easily be reduced. 

They amount to 26 percent. So, the maximum practical efficiency of this or similar designs cannot much exceed 74 percent. 

An experimental unit under test has given 65 percent, corresponding to a daily water yield of 1.8 pounds per square foot from a water layer 0.36 inch deep. Such a simple flat-plate solar still is suitable for the Tropics where the sun is always overhead.

In the temperate zone a flat-plate still with a black back, angled so as to reflect solar rays, has produced about a quart of water per day per square foot, in Cambridge, Mass. 

In the Tropics an acre of evaporator pan should produce about 8,000 gallons of water daily. 

The cost analysis is uncertain. The chief cost would be the annual charges on the capital investment, although the maintenance and operating costs would not be low. Based on Abbot's judgment, a 100,000 kilowatt plant would consist of some 

25,000 tracking mirrors each about 13 feet by 20 feet, and 25,- 000 boilers preferably consisting of vacuum-sheathed glass focus units. Associated storage would be required to carry the load overnight and on cloudy days.

At present, large-scale energy from plants of this kind does not appear to be economical in the United States. 

Hottel has discussed a flat-plate collector for power. Assuming a collector in Phoenix, Ariz., tilted southward at 27 degrees, and consisting of four glass plates, iron-free, with one-fourth wave-length coatings, the edges factory-sealed and the spaces filled with a special gas, operating at the optimum temperature Page 217

of degrees Fahrenheit, he estimates the electricity generated would cost about 2 cents a kilowatt-hour. About 200 square feet of collector would be required for each kilowatt (during daylight) corresponding to some 240 horsepower per acre—an over-all efficiency of about 6 percent in the conversion of sunlight to electricity. 

Daniels has proposed various other devices-plastic bags filled with water as focussing lenses; the use of brown nitrogen dioxide as a light-absorbing, chemically dissociating gas; a solar engine using a reciprocating light and shadow arrangement.

Doubtless many other possibilities would be revealed by aggressive research.

EXTRACTING ENERGY FROM THE WINDS 

An experimental 1,250-kilowatt Smith-Putnam wind turbine was built on Grandpa's Knob in Vermont in 1940. The stainless steel blades swept an area 187 feet in diameter. The unit generated alternating current, and fed into the lines of the Central Vermont Public Service Co. 

In the course of 5 years of experiments, the engineers in charge concluded that the major mechanical problems had been solved, and that a unit could be designed to remain safely on line in any wind.

Several hundred cost studies were made. It was concluded that the economically optimum wind-turbine would stand about 165 feet high, with a diameter of about 225 feet and a rating of about 2,000 kilowatts-virtually regardless of the wind regime. Shifting patterns in the cost of materials would alter these values somewhat.

The energy in the wind varies as the cube of its velocity. 

Below 18 miles an hour, there is very little energy. To be economically attractive in the United States, a wind regime must have an average annual velocity of some 28 miles an hour or more at hub-height. In countries where energy costs are higher than in the United States, less vigorous wind regimes would be sources of economically recoverable energy.

The British now have an experimental 100-kilowatt unit under way in Scotland, where the average annual velocity may be not far from 30 miles an hour. The coal-short German city of Salach is also reported to be building a 100-kilowatt windturbine.

The Russians had a 3-bladed 100-kilowatt unit on a hill near Yalta before the war, feeding into the 20,000-kilowatt peatburning steam-station at Sebastopol.

Attractive wind-power sites are at least as rare as good dam sites. For example, what is needed in New England, where the prevailing wind flow is from the west, is a ridge trending north-south, with favorable and regular aerodynamic characteristics to increase the average annual velocity of the "free-air" flow, and long enough to support a battery of at least ten 2,500 kilowatt units-that is, several miles long. There are not many such ridges in New England, or anywhere else. An ultimate installed capacity in excess of 25 million kilowatts seems doubtful.

During the next century we may obtain from the wind a cumulative world total of energy equivalent to 3,800 million tons of bituminous coal.

ENERGY FROM HEAT DIFFERENCES IN TROPICAL WATERS 

Along some, but not all, tropical coasts, the hot surface water is closely underlain by cold water. Regions are known where there is a temperature difference of as much as 30 degrees Fahrenheit within 5,000 feet of the surface, quite close to shore. 

Such differences between "limitless" masses of water suggest that great quantities of energy could be obtained from the relatively high thermal potential.

Georges Claude made the first attempt to obtain this energy in 1930 off Havana. His apparatus was wrecked by a gale.

The French Government is trying again, off the Gold Coast of West Africa, near Abidjan. Two 3,500-kilowatt units are planned. Components were successfully tested full-scale in the sea off Marseilles in September 1947.

The cycle is as follows: The warm surface water is evaporated under vacuum. This "steam" is "inhaled" by the condenser, cooled by the deep water. On its passage, the “steam" passes through the turbine of an electric generator. The motive force is generated by the difference in the absolute vapor pressures of the "steam" at 82 degrees Fahrenheit and the condensate at 48 degrees Fahrenheit.

The process may also be used as a source of energy for the evaporating plant in chemical industries and in artificial salines. 

The French consider that the ultimate potential economics of thermal sea-energy compares favorably with much landborne hydro.

But suitable sites close to storm-free tropical coasts with cold water not too deep and not too far off shore, and close to load centers, are not as common as are hydroelectric sites. 

Perhaps, over the next 100 years, we might hope for onefourth as much energy from temperature differences of the sea as from hydro, requiring an installed capacity of one or two hundred million kilowatts.

ENERGY FROM CONTROLLED BIOLOGICAL PHOTOSYNTHESIS 

Biological photosynthesis is the process by which a pigment, like chlorophyll, uses the energy of sunlight to reduce water, and the carbon dioxide of the atmosphere, releasing oxygen and locking up carbon in a series of fats, proteins, sugars, starches, and other carbohydrates, in various parts of the plant. 

These reaction-products may in turn be processed into an endless variety of things-pharmaceuticals, food for livestock and human beings, fuel, clothing, and other materials. 

Of the solar energy that reaches the outer atmosphere of the earth in an average year, the amount that gets through to the earth's surface is equivalent to about 120,000 billion tons of bituminous coal. Approximately 30 percent of this energy reaches land areas outside of the Arctic and the Antarctic regions. The carbon that is fixed by photosynthesis in the sea each year is many times as great as the quantity fixed on land. 

However, the calculations in this draft memorandum will be concerned solely with the problem of making use of that fraction of solar energy which strikes the land surfaces. Page 218

Not all this solar energy is suitable for photosynthesis. Energy of wavelength shorter than about 4,000 Angstroms*-ultraviolet light—or longer than about 10,000 Angstroms-infrared light-does not appear to play a part in any photosynthesis process yet discovered. This totals about 20 percent of the energy in the solar spectrum as it reaches the earth's land surface-4 percent below 4,000 Angstroms and 16 percent above 10,000. It is either reflected, or absorbed and converted to heat. 

At most, 80 percent can enter into some one of the several processes of biological photosynthesis, although no one process is yet known that can utilize energy over the whole range from the ultra-violet to the infra-red-from 4,000 to 10,000 Angstroms.

The efficiency of biological photosynthesis—that is, the efficiency with which light energy is converted into the heat of combustion of dry algae-has a theoretical maximum lying in the range 25 to 35 percent. The practical maximum is yet to be established.

If we take 30 percent as the ultimate practical value—and there is little reason today to believe that this figure can be reached-we find that the total reserve of solar energy falling on land surfaces each year, which might be converted to fats, proteins, sugars, starches, and other carbohydrates, is equivalent to about 8,740 billion tons of bituminous coal. 

Of this energy that is potentially available for all forms of photosynthetic fixation of carbon, about 45 percent falls in the visible spectrum—the portion that the chlorophylls can use. 

The total tonnage of carbon annually fixed on land today would, if burned, yield energy equivalent to that of about 12 billion tons of bituminous coal, which is little more than four times the total input to the world's energy system in 1950. The margin, based on present practices, appears uncomfortably small. What can be done about the 700-fold spread between the present performance and the theoretically "possible” performance of an 8,740-billion-ton bituminous coal equivalent?

TESTS MADE WITH CHLORELLA 

Recent work on Chlorella-a single-celled green alga seen in ponds has begun to give the answer, which is not hopeful. 

Chlorella grown under laboratory and pilot-plant conditions indicates a yearly acre yield of some 35 tons of a dark-green powder, which is normally 50 percent protein. Acre for acre, this is about 100 times as productive as soy beans, the richest common source of vegetable protein. However, there is some uncertainty about the kind of protein in Chlorella. Comprehensive animal feeding experiments can be expected to clear up this point.

The composition of Chlorella can be varied at will, by controlling the environment. Either high protein-up to 55 percent-or high fat-up to 85 percent can be obtained. To date, a high fat content has implied a slow growth-rate. 

Chlorella, when burned, gives up 9,000 to 13,000 B. t. u. per pound,† depending on the proportions of fat, protein, and carbohydrates. 

The costs of large-scale Chlorella farming are not yet known. 

Nutrients include trace elements and nitrogen in the form of *An Angstrom is a unit of measurement of light waves, equal to onehundred millionth of a centimeter. †The weighted average heat content of a pound of bituminous coal in the United States is 13,100 B. t. u. ammonia. The cost of these nutrients is estimated to come to about one-half cent a pound of dry Chlorella. The carbon dioxide, which is maintained at a concentration of about 5 percent, costs another one-half cent for each pound of dry Chlorella. Pumping the solution, harvesting it by centrifuging the 

Chlorella, drying the Chlorella, labor, and supervision, and other annual charges bring the total cost to about 27 cents a pound for Chlorella, as estimated by A. D. Little, Inc., for a 

10-acre plant yielding 6 tons a day and based on the pilot-plant studies conducted at Cambridge, Mass., in 1951-52 for the 

Carnegie Institution of Washington.

Elsewhere we have said that a source of energy would be acceptable if its real unit costs did not exceed about 1.5 times the present real unit costs of energy. So, if energy from a 

Chlorella-like organism is to be satisfactory, the harvest should not cost over 0.4 cent a pound dry-weight-less than onesixtieth any costs now in sight. Ultimately, 10 cents a pound may be achieved. But a figure of 5 cents a pound, while not impossible, is extremely optimistic. And even this figure is 10 times too high for our needs.

The prospect of reaching any such cost as 0.4 cent a pound dry weight for Chlorella does not appear bright. However, there are several possibilities to explore. 

Chlorella is one of some 17,500 related organisms. Of this total, about 10,000 appear suitable at first glance for mass farming. They are at least worth further exploration. Barely 

400 are represented in the only type-collection in existencethat of Pringsheim of Cambridge University, England; and of these, only Chlorella has been investigated in any detail. Based on experience to date, it seems likely that each species will yield anywhere from 10 to 50 strains, often with widely divergent characteristics between strains.

The 10,000 species thought to be suitable for further investigation are those already discovered. There is not much of a clue concerning the number that remain to be discovered. 

Most of the 10,000 have been found in the Temperate Zone and in accessible places. No comprehensive search of the planet has been made. It has been estimated that such a search might yield as many more again, and that these, in turn, would yield many strains. It is possible, therefore, that the total number of natural wild forms to be investigated may comprise many hundreds of thousands of strains.

Among these hundreds of thousands of strains there may be found some that will help close the gap between the presently estimated costs of 27 cents a pound dry-weight and the target of 0.4 cent a pound.

SOLAR POWER OUTPUT METHODS 

If unlike metals are joined together, and if one joint is heated and the other cooled, an electric current is generated. The voltage is low. Telkes at M. I. T. has sought alloys with optimum combinations of high thermo-electric power, low electrical resistance and low thermal conductivity. She has found that when the positive alloy is zinc-antimony plus small amounts of tin or silver, and the negative alloy is galena (lead sulfide) plus excess lead, she obtains a useful conversion of 7 percent when operating between 420 and 20 degrees centigrade. This combination yields nearly 400 microvolts per degree centigrade. Page 219

Miles of such wire, coiled back and forth over an acre, would consume large quantities of vanishing metals. And the hot junctions would have to be heated by tracking mirrors like those of Abbot. By comparison Abbot estimates an over-all efficiency at the drive shaft of his generator of some 16 percent.

There is hope that new types of thermo-piles can be found, operating at much higher efficiencies, and consisting of lowcost materials. While cut-and-try methods might be rewarding, new theories might open up new possibilities.

STORAGE OF LIGHT IN PHOSPHORS 

Phosphors are substances that can absorb radiant energy and re-radiate it after a lapse of time. Westinghouse engineers look to the day when much of our lighting will come from special phosphor powders in paints and wall papers. Clear daylight varies from about 2,400 foot-candles in winter to about 8,000 in summer. At night a well-lighted room requires about 

100 foot-candles.

If we could develop a phosphor that would radiate at night from 1 to 5 percent of the light it received by day, our lighting load, which amounts to about 5 percent of the total energy system, could be carried directly by the sun. 

Other possibilities still in the earliest stages of development include: a) Solar power from photo-voltaic cells. b) Production of energy in oxidation-reduction systems. c) Photochemical decomposition of water. d) Storage of heat in crystal lattices. e) Nonbiological photosynthesis.

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS 

The reserves of fuels with which to meet energy demands are relative. It is not a question of emptying the bin. We shall never do that. It is a question of how far down it is worth reaching in terms of economic cost. Such a question has no exact answer. 

If growing populations in the United States and throughout the free world are to make ever greater per capital demands for the output of energy, while avoiding further serious increases in unit costs, then alternative low-cost sources of energy should be made ready to pick up some of the load by about 1975. 

Nuclear fuels, for various technical reasons, are unlikely ever to bear more than about one-fifth of the load.*

We must look to solar energy. Solar energy is available as shown in table VIII.

TABLE VIII. The annual supply of solar energy 

Thus, the solar energy reaching the United States is some 1,500 times the input to the national energy system in 1950. 

Mere improvements in open agriculture will not give us the economical energy sources we shall need. Today in the United 

States food-energy comes to about 3 percent of total energy consumed. By 1975 it may be only 2 percent. The yield from open agriculture can perhaps be doubled or quadrupled. It can hardly be multiplied by 50 or more. a) Among the means of harnessing solar energy are: 

Solar hot-water heaters, the heat-pump, solar or otherwise, and solar-house-heating and air-conditioning systems, all of which are already either in economic production or on the verge of it. b) Controlled biological photosynthesis, while it is a promising source of foods, drugs, and a wide range of synthetic materials, does not yet look very promising as an economic source of energy. c) Various means of physically converting sunlight into sources of large-scale useful energy have been proposed. 

Some are technically feasible, but costly; some are theoretically possible, but need basic development to become practical; and some are doubtless awaiting the accident of scientific discovery.

Efforts made to date to harness solar energy economically are infinitesimal. It is time for aggressive research in the whole field of solar energy-an effort in which the United States could make an immense contribution to the welfare of the free world.
